rows.question: How do I change the address on my driving licence?
keyFacts: It does not cost anything to change your address with DVLA
You can apply online (or by post)

answer.answer:
You can change the address on your full or provisional GB driving licence online or by post, free of charge (you only pay if you also want a new photo).

Online: sign in to your GOV.UK account and follow the "change address" service (you may need to prove your identity with photo ID). You'll get a confirmation email, and the licence should arrive within a week. You can keep driving while you wait. If you want to change your name at the same time, you must apply by post instead.

By post:
- Photocard licence: complete the "changes" section on letter D741 that came with your licence, then send the licence and the letter to DVLA, Swansea, SA99 1BN. If you don't have the D741, use form D1 (car/motorcycle) or D2 (lorry/bus), available at most Post Offices.
- Paper licence: send a completed D1 (or D2 for lorry/bus), your licence, original documents confirming your identity, and a passport photograph.
Allow up to 3 weeks; contact DVLA if it hasn't arrived by then. Pay the correct postage.

Also: update your vehicle log book (V5C), your vehicle tax Direct Debit if you pay that way, and your personalised registration document (V750 or V778) if you have one. You can be fined up to £1,000 if you don't tell DVLA about an address change.

If you're moving abroad, you can't change the address on a British licence; contact the licensing authority in your new country. Northern Ireland has a different process.

rows.question: How long do penalty points stay on my licence?
keyFacts: Penalty points/endorsements stay on your driving record for 4 or 11 years, depending on the offence

answer.answer: It depends on the offence. Most penalty points (endorsements) stay on your driving record for 4 years from the date of the offence. Reckless/dangerous driving endorsements (DD40, DD60, DD80) and those resulting in disqualification stay for 4 years from the date of conviction. Drink or drug driving (DR10, DR20, DR30, DR31, DR61, DR80) and causing death by careless driving while under the influence (CD40, CD50, CD60) or failing to provide a specimen (CD70) stay for 11 years from the date of conviction. Totting-up code TT99 stays for 4 years from conviction. Your penalty points are only "valid" for the first 3 years (4-year endorsement) or 10 years (11-year endorsement), and insurers and employers may see them for longer. You can check when points will be removed on your driving licence record.

rows.question: How do I tell DVLA my car is off the road?
keyFacts: Tell DVLA online (or by phone/post) that the vehicle is off the road: a SORN
You get a refund for any full months of remaining tax

answer.answer:
You tell DVLA by making a SORN (Statutory Off Road Notification), which registers the vehicle as off the road. Options:

- Online: available if the vehicle is registered in your name. Have your 11-digit V5C (log book) number or the 16-digit reference from your vehicle tax reminder (V11 letter, email or text) ready. You can start when you're ready to take the vehicle off the road.
- By phone: DVLA vehicle service on 0300 123 4321 (24-hour service).
- By post: send a V890 form to DVLA, Swansea, SA99 1AR. You can apply this month, or next month or the month after, but if sending it early include a letter explaining why you can't send it nearer the time.

If the vehicle isn't registered in your name, fill in the appropriate part of the log book and send it with the V890. If you don't have a log book, send a V62 application (£25 for a new log book) with the V890.

Timing: the SORN starts immediately if your vehicle tax has already expired or you're not applying in the month tax is due to expire. If you apply in the tax expiry month, it starts on the first day of the next month. You'll get a refund for any full months of remaining tax, but you can't use the vehicle on the road until you tax it again. If you've sold the vehicle, tell DVLA about the sale instead of making a SORN.

rows.question: Which vehicles are exempt from vehicle tax?
keyFacts: Historic vehicles built before 1 January 1986 are exempt from vehicle tax
Vehicles used by a disabled person can be exempt
Electric cars are no longer exempt: from 1 April 2025 they must pay vehicle tax

answer.answer:
Vehicles exempt from vehicle tax (you must still tax them, even though no payment is due) include:
- Vehicles used by a disabled person (claimed when applying for tax; one vehicle at a time)
- Vehicles (except ambulances) used by organisations providing transport for disabled people
- Historic vehicles made before 1 January 1986 (must apply to be exempt)
- Mobility vehicles and powered wheelchairs with a maximum speed of 8mph and a device limiting them to 4mph on footways
- Electric vehicles: from 1 April 2025 electric cars, vans, motorcycles and tricycles must pay tax; only heavy goods vehicles over 3,500kg remain exempt. Hybrid electric vehicles must pay.
- Mowing machines designed and used for cutting grass only (not tractors towing gang mowers)
- Steam-powered vehicles
- Vehicles used for agriculture, horticulture and forestry, such as tractors, agricultural engines, light agricultural vehicles used off-road, and 'limited use' vehicles making short trips (up to 1.5km) on a public road between land used by the same person

Vehicles registered as off the road (SORN) get a refund for unused tax already paid, but this is not an exemption category.

rows.question: How do I check the MOT history of a car?
keyFacts: You need the vehicle's number plate (registration number)
The history shows past pass/fail results, recorded mileage and when the next MOT is due

answer.answer:
Use the GOV.UK "Check the MOT history of a vehicle" service and enter the vehicle's number plate (registration number). It shows past test results (pass or fail), the recorded mileage, and when the next MOT is due, and may show safety recall information depending on the manufacturer.

Extra details:
- For tests in England, Scotland or Wales you can also download current and previous MOT certificates, see where each test was done (you'll need the 11-digit number from the V5C log book), and see which parts failed or had minor problems.
- Results are available for cars, motorcycles and vans for tests since 2005 (HGVs, trailers, buses and coaches since 2018).
- For tests in Northern Ireland, results are available since 2017, but certificates can't be downloaded here. If the MOT is still valid, you can apply for a duplicate certificate on NI Direct; duplicates aren't available for expired MOTs.

rows.question: What do I need to do when I sell my car?
keyFacts: Tell DVLA you've sold or transferred the vehicle
You get a refund for any full months of vehicle tax left

answer.answer:
When you sell a car, you need to tell DVLA that you no longer own it:

1. Tell DVLA online (gov.uk "Tell DVLA you've sold, transferred or bought a vehicle"). This changes the registered keeper and sends the log book (V5C) to the new keeper. Your vehicle tax is cancelled and you get a refund for any full months left. The online service is not available if you have already posted the V5C or don't have a log book.
2. Give the buyer the V5C log book. If you have the new-style log book (multi-coloured numbered blocks), fill in section 2; if it's the older style, fill in section 6 (and sign the declaration in section 8). Give the green 'new keeper' slip to the buyer, then send the V5C to DVLA.
3. If you don't have the log book, write to DVLA (Swansea SA99 1BA) with: your name and address, the registration number, make and model, the exact date of sale, and the new keeper's or motor trader's name and address. The buyer will need to apply for a new V5C using form V62 (£25 fee).
4. If you sell to a motor trader, fill in the yellow 'sell, transfer or part-exchange your vehicle to the motor trade' section of the log book and send the perforated section to DVLA.

The buyer must tax the vehicle before driving it (tax isn't transferred), or declare it off the road with a SORN.

rows.question: What should I do if my car has been stolen?
keyFacts: Tell the police (dial 101) and your insurance company straight away
If the insurer pays out, you must tell DVLA the vehicle has been sold to the insurer

answer.answer:
1. Report it to the police straight away by calling 101 and asking for your local police. Have the registration number, make and model, and colour ready. You'll get a crime reference number, which you need for your insurer. The police will tell DVLA about the theft.
2. Call your insurance company straight away, give them the crime reference number, and they'll tell you how to make a claim.
3. If your insurer pays out, you must tell DVLA the vehicle has been sold to the insurance company. You can do this online, or by filling in the yellow 'sell, transfer or part-exchange to the motor trade' section of the log book and sending the perforated section to DVLA with a letter (the date the payment was accepted and your insurer's details). Send the rest of the log book to your insurer. If the insurer asks for the whole log book, write to DVLA (Swansea, SA99 1BD) with your insurer's details, the claim date, registration number, make, model, colour and your signature.
4. If the car had a private (personalised) registration number you want to keep, apply to keep it as soon as the car is stolen, within 2 years and 6 months of telling DVLA. You can only get it back if you told the police, and the car had a valid MOT and up-to-date vehicle tax when it was stolen. Only after you get the number back should you tell DVLA you no longer own the vehicle.

rows.question: What are the penalties for speeding?
keyFacts: The minimum penalty is a £100 fine and 3 penalty points
You could be disqualified if you reach 12 or more points within 3 years

answer.answer:
The minimum penalty for speeding is a £100 fine and 3 penalty points on your licence. You could be disqualified if you build up 12 or more penalty points within 3 years.

- If you plead guilty: you pay the £100 fine and get 3 points, unless you're offered a speed awareness course. You can be offered one if the police consider it appropriate and you haven't been on one in the past 3 years. Your licence will show a code for 4 years.
- If you plead not guilty: you go to court. If found guilty, you can be fined more and get more points. The fine is usually a percentage of your weekly income, up to a maximum of £1,000 (£2,500 if on a motorway). You could also be disqualified or have your licence suspended.
- Police stopping you can give a verbal warning, give or send you a fixed penalty notice, or order you to go to court.
- Speeding offence codes (SP10–SP50) carry 3 to 6 penalty points, and stay on your driving record for 4 years from the offence date.

rows.question: How do I get my licence back after a driving ban?
keyFacts: You must apply for a new licence to drive again
For drink or drug driving you can reapply before the disqualification ends, using the D27 form DVLA sends

answer.answer:
You can't drive until the disqualification period has ended. Then:

1. Check when your ban ends using your driving record online.
2. Get a new licence application. DVLA normally sends a D27 renewal form 56 days before the ban ends (90 days if you're a high risk offender). If it doesn't arrive, get form D1 (car/motorbike) or D2 (lorry/bus) from a Post Office that offers DVLA services.
3. Complete the form, send it to DVLA with the licence fee (and a passport-style photo if the D27 says you need one).
4. If the court told you to retake your driving test, you'll need to apply for a new provisional licence and pass the theory and practical tests (an extended practical test if the court required it) before you can drive again. You can drive as soon as you've passed the practical test.
5. If you want to drive a lorry or bus (categories C or D), the traffic commissioner must agree; DVLA asks them when you apply.

Notes: if your licence was revoked and you're a new driver (licence cancelled within 2 years of passing your test), you must reapply for a provisional licence and retake both parts of the test. In Northern Ireland, contact the Driver and Vehicle Agency (DVA) instead. Non-GB licence holders get their licence returned by DVLA when the disqualification ends.

rows.question: Can I drive if I have diabetes?

- Diet-only treatment: you do not need to tell DVLA.

rows.question: What are the eyesight rules for driving?
keyFacts: You must be able to read a number plate from 20 metres away
Minimum visual acuity of decimal 0.5 (6/12) on the Snellen scale, with glasses or contact lenses if needed

answer.answer:
Car drivers (standard licence):
- You must be able to read a number plate from 20 metres away. Glasses or contact lenses are allowed, and you must wear them every time you drive if you need them to meet the standard.
- Visual acuity must be at least decimal 0.5 (6/12) on the Snellen scale, using both eyes together, or in the one eye if you have sight in only one eye (with glasses or contact lenses if needed).
- You must have an adequate field of vision. An optician can check this.

Lorry and bus drivers (higher standard):
- Visual acuity of at least 0.8 (6/7.5) in the best eye and at least 0.1 (6/60) in the other.
- Glasses up to (+) 8 dioptres, or contact lenses, can be used to meet this.
- An uninterrupted horizontal visual field of at least 160 degrees, extending at least 70 degrees left and right and 30 degrees up and down, with no defects within a radius of the central 30 degrees.
- Drivers who held a lorry or bus licence before 1 January 1997 may still be able to renew if they cannot meet these standards.

Reporting: you must tell DVLA about any eyesight problem affecting both eyes (or your only eye). Short sight, long sight and colour blindness do not need to be reported, and nor does surgery to correct short sight if you meet the standards. Lorry and bus drivers must report a problem affecting either eye.

Tests: you must read a number plate on a parked vehicle at the start of your practical driving test, or the test will not continue. If you have your eyesight test done by an optician elsewhere, it must include an Esterman visual test, and DVLA does not guarantee it will accept it. Failing to meet the standards while driving can lead to prosecution.

rows.question: What do the codes on my driving licence mean?
keyFacts: The codes on the back of the licence set conditions you must meet to drive
Examples: 01 eyesight correction (glasses or contact lenses); 78 automatic transmission only

answer.answer:
The codes on the back of your licence show the conditions you must meet to drive (some differ in Northern Ireland). The most common ones:

- 01: wear glasses or contact lenses
- 02: use a hearing or communication aid
- 78 or 106: automatic transmission only
- 79: vehicle must match the specification in brackets on the licence
- 96: vehicle and trailer where the trailer weighs at least 750kg and the combined weight is 3,500–4,250kg
- 101: not for hire or reward (not to make a profit)
- 115: organ donor
- 70 or 71: the licence is an exchange or a duplicate

Vehicle adaptation codes show modifications needed to drive safely: 10 (modified transmission), 15 (clutch), 20 (braking), 25 (accelerator), 31 (pedal adaptations), 35 (control layouts), 40 (steering), 42 (mirrors), 43 (driving seat), and 44 with sub-codes for motorbike adaptations, plus 45 (motorbikes with sidecar only).

Other restrictions include: 97 (not C1 vehicles needing a tachograph), 102 (drawbar trailers only), 103 (certificate of competence), 105 (vehicle no more than 5.5m long), 107 (no more than 8,250kg), 108 (minimum age requirements), 110 (restricted-mobility passengers), 111 and 113 (16 passenger seats), 114 (special controls), 118 (earliest entitlement start date), 119 (no weight limit for vehicle), 121 (conditions in the Secretary of State's notice), 122 (Basic Moped Training Course completed, not trial e-scooters), and 125 (tricycles only, pre-29 June 2014 licences).

Codes 30 and 46 are older codes for licences issued before 28 November 2016 and 29 June 2014 respectively.

Your category letters (such as B or C1) are separate from these codes. Penalty point codes such as LC20 or MR49 record offences on your driving record, not conditions on the licence.

rows.question: How do I swap my paper driving licence for a photocard?
keyFacts: You do not need to exchange a valid paper licence unless you change your address or name, want to do Driver CPC training, or it is damaged, lost or stolen
It is free if you changed your name or address and still have the paper licence
Otherwise a new photocard licence costs £20

answer.answer:
You only need to exchange a paper licence if it is defaced, lost, stolen or destroyed, or if you've changed your address or name, or want to do Driver CPC training. If your paper licence is still valid and none of these apply, you don't need to exchange it.

- Online: sign in to the DVLA service to renew/exchange online. You must be a resident of Great Britain, not disqualified or prevented from driving, and meet the minimum eyesight requirement. Online applications are not possible if you've changed your name. The fee is £20 if the licence was defaced, lost, stolen or destroyed, or for any other reason; it's free if you've only changed your name or address and still have your paper licence. You can pay by Mastercard, Visa, Electron or Delta.
- By post (if you've changed your name, or can't apply online): complete form D1 (cars and motorbikes) or D2 (buses and lorries), available from most Post Offices. Include your original identity documents, a colour passport-type photo, and the £20 fee if applicable (cheques or postal orders payable to DVLA; no cash). Send ccar and motorbike applications to DVLA, Swansea, SA99 1BU, or bus and lorry applications to DVLA, Swansea, SA99 1BR.

DVLA aims to send the new licence within 3 weeks, possibly longer if medical or personal details need checking. If you've applied, you may be able to keep driving under the previous licence's conditions while you wait, if you meet all the listed conditions (including having your doctor's support where relevant).

rows.question: How do I change my driving test appointment?
keyFacts: You can change a car driving test only 2 times

answer.answer:
You must change your car driving test yourself, online, using the DVSA driving test booking service (available 6am to 11:40pm). Your driving instructor cannot do it for you. You'll need at least 2 of: your UK driving licence number, your theory test pass certificate number, or your driving test booking reference.

What you can do: find an earlier (cancellation) appointment, move the test to a later date, or change the test centre to a nearby one. Changing the date, time or centre counts as one change even if you change more than one thing at once.

Limits: the change-driving-test page says you can change a car test 2 times. A separate GOV.UK page on the 2026 booking rules says you get 2 changes, and that only you can make them, and it mentions moving only to nearby centres. Those two pages don't fully agree on the limit for non-car tests (the first says 6), so check the booking service for what it allows you.

Notice: to change for free you need 10 full working days' notice for a car test (3 for other tests). Monday to Saturday count as working days; Sundays and public holidays don't. Changing to a weekend, evening or bank holiday slot means paying the price difference; moving to a weekday slot gets a refund of the difference. If you can't find a suitable slot, you can cancel instead, with the same notice to get a refund.

Short notice: if something unavoidable happened (illness or injury, bereavement, a school or college exam, or a stolen licence), you can ask for a short-notice refund by emailing customerservices@dvsa.gov.uk with the subject "Unavoidable short notice cancellation", attaching proof and including at least 2 of your reference details.

New appointments are released 24 weeks ahead every Monday at 6am, and cancellation appointments appear at any time. There is no waiting list.

rows.question: How do I tax a car if I haven't received a tax reminder?
keyFacts: You can tax online with the 11-digit reference number from your V5C (or the 12-digit number on the green new keeper slip)
You can also tax by phone or at a Post Office

answer.answer:
You don't need a reminder letter (V11), email or text to tax your car. Use one of these documents:
- Current keeper: your V5C logbook (11-digit reference number) in your name. If you don't have one, apply for a V62 (or a replacement V5C, £25) and you can tax at the same time.
- New keeper who has just bought the car: the green 'new keeper' slip (12-digit reference number). You can't tax without it, so if you don't have it you must apply for a new V5C by post (£25).

Ways to tax:
- Online: using the 11-digit V5C reference (current keeper) or 12-digit new keeper slip reference.
- By phone: call DVLA on 0300 123 4321 with your V5C or new keeper slip to hand.
- At a Post Office that deals with vehicle tax: bring your V5C, V62 or new keeper slip, payment, and if you need it, evidence of a current MOT (e.g. MOT history screenshot or certificate). You can also set up a Direct Debit there (bring your address, date of birth and bank details).
- In Northern Ireland, you also need a valid MOT certificate when the tax starts and an insurance certificate or cover note.

You can check online afterwards that the vehicle has been taxed.

rows.question: I've just bought a used car. What do I need to do to tax it and get it registered in my name?

rows.question: My car is over 40 years old. Does it need an MOT, and does it need vehicle tax?
keyFacts: No MOT is needed if the vehicle was built or first registered more than 40 years ago and not substantially changed
Vehicles built before 1 January 1986 are exempt from vehicle tax

answer.answer:

You still must keep it roadworthy; you can be fined up to £2,500 and get 3 penalty points for using a vehicle in a dangerous condition.

Vehicle tax: Being over 40 years old does not by itself remove the need for tax. Tax depends on the build date: if your car was built before 1 January 1986 (or, if you don't know the build date, first registered before 8 January 1986), you can apply to stop paying vehicle tax from 1 April 2026 under the historic tax class. You must still tax it (at no cost) and cannot be used for hire or reward or for a trade or business. To apply, take the V5C log book, any V11 reminder, and evidence of MOT or MOT exemption (V112) to a Post Office that deals with vehicle tax. Driving untaxed can be fined £80. A car over 40 years old but built after 1985 would not qualify for the tax exemption and would need to be taxed as normal.

rows.question: I'm 17 and want to learn to drive. What licence and tests do I need, and what do they cost?
keyFacts: You can apply for a provisional licence from 15 years and 9 months (£34 online)
You must pass a theory test (£23) and a driving test (£62 weekdays)
You can usually start driving a car at 17

answer.answer:
To learn to drive a car at 17 in Great Britain you need:

1. A provisional driving licence. Apply online at GOV.UK (you must be at least 15 years 9 months old, able to read a number plate from 20 metres, and have been given permission to live in Great Britain for at least 185 days). It costs £34 online, or £43 by post using form D1.

2. A car theory test (you must have your provisional licence to book it). It has two parts, multiple-choice questions and hazard perception, and you must pass both in one sitting. It costs £23.

3. A practical driving test, booked once you've passed the theory test. It costs £62 on weekdays, or £75 in evenings, at weekends and on bank holidays. There's no minimum number of lessons; you should only book when you can drive safely without instruction and show you know the Highway Code.

While learning you must display L plates, be supervised by a qualified driver (an approved driving instructor, or a family member or friend who is 21+, has held a full licence for 3+ years, and is not banned), and have insurance covering you. You can drive at any time of day, but you can only drive on motorways with an approved driving instructor in a car with dual controls. Driving without insurance can bring an unlimited fine, a ban and up to 8 penalty points. Supervisors may not accept any payment, including for fuel.

Approximate total for the licence and tests: £34 + £23 + £62 (or £75), before lessons and insurance. Booking through GOV.UK is the official price; unofficial sites usually charge more.

rows.question: My car has been written off. What do I tell DVLA and what happens to my vehicle tax?
keyFacts: You must tell DVLA the vehicle was written off and scrapped by your insurer
You get a vehicle tax refund for any full months left

answer.answer:
Tell DVLA online at GOV.UK (Mon–Fri 7am–9pm, Sat–Sun 7am–8pm), or by post. You'll need: your insurer's name and postcode (under 'provide trader details'), the vehicle registration number, and the 11-digit reference from the yellow 'sell, transfer or part-exchange to the motor trade' section of the V5C log book. Check the name and address on the log book are correct (apply by post if not), and remove any personalised registration number. Destroy the yellow section once finished (don't send it to DVLA); your insurer will ask for the rest of the log book. Failing to tell DVLA can mean a £1,000 fine.

Vehicle tax: telling DVLA cancels your vehicle tax. You'll get a refund for any full months left, calculated from the date DVLA receives your information, sent as a cheque to the name and address on the log book. If you pay by Direct Debit, it's cancelled automatically. You won't get refunds for credit card fees, the 5% Direct Debit surcharge, or the 10% surcharge on a single 6-month payment.

You'll then receive an email (if you gave one) and a letter confirming you're no longer the keeper.

rows.question: I'm over 70 and have a medical condition. How do I renew my driving licence?
keyFacts: You can renew online for free from 70 if you meet the eyesight requirement and nothing prevents you from driving
You must tell DVLA about medical conditions that affect your driving

answer.answer:
If you're 70 or over and have a medical condition, you renew the same way as other drivers aged 70+, but you must declare the condition:

1. Apply online (free) at GOV.UK, or by post using form D46P. DVLA sends the D46P automatically 90 days before your 70th birthday or licence expiry. You can also use a D1 form from most Post Offices if you don't have the D46P. Online, you'll need to sign in and may need to prove your identity with photo ID. Postal applications can take about 3 weeks, longer if your medical details need checking.
2. Tell DVLA about any notifiable condition in the application form. You don't need to contact DVLA separately. Notifiable conditions include things like diabetes, heart conditions, sleep apnoea, epilepsy, strokes, glaucoma and fainting (syncope). Failing to declare one can lead to a fine of up to £1,000.
3. Meet the eyesight requirement. You can only use the online service if you meet the minimum eyesight standard and are not prevented from driving for any reason.
4. Expect possible follow-up. DVLA may contact your doctor, arrange an examination, or ask for a driving assessment. It may also issue a shorter licence (1, 2, 3 or 5 years) or require adaptations. Your application may take longer if it's referred to a doctor.

Once you reach 70, you must renew every 3 years. If you have a C1 or D1 entitlement, you must renew it by post.

You can usually keep driving while DVLA considers your application if you have your doctor's support, your last licence wasn't revoked or refused for medical reasons, and your application is less than a year old. If you've been told to stop driving, you can't renew this way. Instead, follow the reapplication process or contact DVLA.

The pages don't say exactly which medical evidence DVLA will need for your specific condition, so check your renewal letter or contact DVLA if you're unsure.
